subjective.question: Describe Sperling's partial report procedure and explain what it revealed about visual sensory memory.
subjective.answer: Sperling presented a grid of 12 letters (3 rows of 4) for a very brief duration (about 50 milliseconds) using a tachistoscope. In the whole report condition, subjects could report only 4-5 letters. In the partial report condition, immediately after the display, a high, medium or low tone indicated which row to report; subjects could report almost all letters of the cued row. This showed that immediately after the display almost all 12 letters were available in visual sensory (iconic) memory, but the information faded within a fraction of a second, before more than a few items could be read out. Iconic memory therefore has a large capacity but a very brief duration.

subjective.question: What is meant by "good form" in Gestalt theory of perception?
subjective.answer: Good form, or Pragnanz, is the Gestalt principle that perceptual organization always tends towards the best, simplest, most regular and most stable form possible under the given conditions. Out of many possible organizations of a stimulus, we perceive the one that is most orderly and meaningful. For example, we perceive a nearly complete circle as a complete circle, and a regular arrangement of dots as rows or columns, because the perceptual system prefers good, regular forms.

subjective.question: Differentiate between recognition and recall.
subjective.answer: In recall, the person has to produce the required item from memory without the item being present, as in essay-type questions or remembering a name on one's own. In recognition, the item itself is presented along with alternatives and the person has to identify the previously learned item, as in multiple-choice questions. Recognition provides retrieval cues, so it is generally easier and more accurate than recall; material that cannot be recalled can often still be recognized.

subjective.question: Compare short-term memory (STM) and long-term memory (LTM) with respect to capacity, duration and coding.
subjective.answer: Capacity: STM is very limited, about 7 plus or minus 2 items, whereas LTM capacity is virtually unlimited. Duration: information in STM is lost within about 18-30 seconds unless rehearsed, whereas LTM can retain information for years or a lifetime. Coding: STM codes information mainly in acoustic (sound-based) form, while LTM codes information mainly in semantic (meaning-based) form. Accuracy: because of its small capacity and rapid forgetting, STM is less accurate for large amounts of material, while LTM stores organized knowledge with greater permanence.

subjective.question: What are the levels of categories? Explain with examples.
subjective.answer: Concepts are organized in hierarchies with three main levels. (1) The superordinate level is the most general, e.g. furniture, animal, vehicle. (2) The basic level is the middle level at which objects are most commonly named and recognized, e.g. chair, dog, car; it carries the most useful information. (3) The subordinate level is the most specific, e.g. dining chair, German shepherd, sports car. We normally think and communicate at the basic level because it is the most informative without being too detailed.

subjective.question: Explain the PQ4R method of studying.
subjective.answer: PQ4R is a method for improving comprehension and retention of written material. Its six steps are: Preview - survey the chapter, headings and summary to get an overview. Question - prepare questions from the headings. Read - read the material actively to answer those questions. Reflect - think about the material, relate it to what you already know and form examples. Recite - recall and state the main points in your own words. Review - go over the material again and check your answers. The method works because it uses elaborative, active processing rather than passive reading.

subjective.question: Describe the Waugh and Norman experiment on forgetting in short-term memory.
subjective.answer: Waugh and Norman presented a series of digits followed by a probe digit; the subject had to recall the digit that had followed the probe digit in the list. By varying the number of items presented after the probe (interfering items) and the speed of presentation, they found that forgetting depended on the number of interfering items rather than on the time elapsed. Their experiment therefore supported the interference theory of STM forgetting: items are lost because other items interfere with them, not simply because their trace decays with time.

subjective.question: What is a schema? Explain with the example of a house.
subjective.answer: A schema is an organized mental framework or structure that represents our knowledge about a concept, object or event, built from past experience. It guides perception, understanding and memory. For example, our schema of a "house" includes its typical parts - walls, roof, doors, windows and rooms - and their usual relations. Because of this schema we can recognize a building as a house even when details differ, fill in missing information, and remember a visited house in terms of what a house is expected to contain.

subjective.question: What is meant by elaborative processing/network? Explain with examples.
subjective.answer: Elaborative processing means learning new material by actively connecting it with knowledge already stored in memory, so the new item becomes part of a rich network of associations. Instead of merely repeating information (maintenance rehearsal), the learner asks what it means, relates it to examples and to his own experience. For example, to remember that Canberra is the capital of Australia, one may connect it with kangaroos, the Sydney Opera House and a map image; the more meaningful links are formed, the more retrieval routes exist and the better the material is remembered.

subjective.question: Briefly describe the visual pathways in the brain.
subjective.answer: Visual information from the retina travels through the optic nerve to the optic chiasm, where fibers from the nasal half of each retina cross to the opposite side. From there the optic tract carries the signals mainly to the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus, and then through the optic radiations to the primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe. Within the cortex, two broad pathways process the information further: a ventral pathway concerned with what an object is (form, color, identity), and a dorsal pathway concerned with where it is (location, movement and guidance of action).

subjective.question: State the main assumptions of Jean Piaget's theory of cognitive development.
subjective.answer: Piaget proposed that children's thinking develops through an invariant sequence of stages (sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational and formal operational). His main assumptions were: children actively construct their knowledge through interaction with the environment; development proceeds through the processes of assimilation (fitting new experiences into existing schemas) and accommodation (modifying schemas to fit new experiences), driven by equilibration; and the child's thought at each stage is qualitatively different from that of adults, not merely less in quantity.

subjective.question: Differentiate between automatic and controlled processes in the context of task interference.
subjective.answer: Controlled processes are slow, serial, effortful and require attention; only one can be carried out at a time, so when two tasks both demand controlled processing they interfere with each other. Automatic processes are fast, parallel and require little or no attention; after sufficient practice a task becomes automatic and can be performed together with another task without interference. For example, an experienced driver can talk while driving because driving has become largely automatic, whereas a beginner cannot.

subjective.question: What did Penfield's experiments demonstrate about memory?
subjective.answer: Wilder Penfield electrically stimulated the exposed cortex of conscious patients during brain surgery. Stimulation of certain temporal-lobe areas made patients vividly re-experience past events - hearing music, voices or scenes from their lives - as if reliving them. These experiments suggested that detailed records of experience are permanently stored in the brain, and that apparently forgotten memories still exist even when they cannot be recalled voluntarily.

subjective.question: Differentiate between the whole report and partial report procedures.
subjective.answer: In the whole report procedure, after a brief visual display the subject tries to report as many items as possible from the whole display; typically only 4-5 out of 12 letters can be reported. In the partial report procedure, a cue presented immediately after the display indicates which part (e.g. one row) is to be reported, and subjects can report almost all items of that part. The comparison shows that the limit in whole report is not the amount initially registered in sensory memory, but the rapid fading of the sensory trace during report.

subjective.question: Define proactive and retroactive interference with examples.
subjective.answer: Interference is the forgetting that occurs because other learning disrupts the memory of the target material. In proactive interference, earlier learning interferes with the learning or recall of later material; e.g. an old telephone number keeps coming to mind and prevents recall of a new one. In retroactive interference, later learning interferes with the recall of earlier material; e.g. after learning a new password, one can no longer recall the previous password. Both types show that forgetting is often caused by competing memories rather than by the passage of time alone.
